questions.question: What is SSH and why is it used with EC2?
questions.answer: SSH (Secure Shell) is an encrypted protocol that allows you to remotely log in to a Linux server and run commands over the internet. EC2 Linux instances do not have a physical keyboard — SSH is how you access them remotely, securely.

questions.question: What are the three methods to connect to a Linux EC2 instance?
questions.answer: 1. EC2 Instance Connect — browser-based, no software needed, AWS injects a temporary key. 2. SSH with .pem key pair — using the terminal on Linux/Mac with chmod 400 on the key. 3. PuTTY — Windows SSH client that requires converting .pem to .ppk using PuTTYgen.

questions.question: Which port must be open in the Security Group for SSH? For RDP?
questions.answer: SSH requires port 22 open as an inbound TCP rule. RDP requires port 3389 open as an inbound TCP rule. These are the most commonly tested ports in AWS exams.

questions.question: What is the difference between stopping and terminating an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: Stopping shuts down the instance but keeps it intact — you can start it again later. Data on EBS volumes is preserved. Terminating permanently deletes the instance — it cannot be recovered. This is the most critical distinction in EC2 management.

questions.question: Why must you run chmod 400 on your .pem file before using it for SSH?
questions.answer: SSH refuses to use private key files that have permissions set too openly — it is a security check. chmod 400 sets the file to read-only for the owner only. Without it, SSH shows 'WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!' and refuses to connect.

questions.question: What is Termination Protection and when should you enable it?
questions.answer: Termination Protection is an EC2 instance attribute that blocks the Terminate action from the console, CLI, or API. You must explicitly disable it before you can terminate the instance. Enable it on any production instance — web servers, databases, or any server you cannot afford to lose permanently.

questions.question: What happens to the public IP address when you stop and start an EC2 instance?
questions.answer: The public IPv4 address is released when the instance is stopped and a different IP is assigned when it starts again. To keep a permanent public IP across stop/start cycles, you must allocate and attach an Elastic IP Address.

questions.question: Name the five EC2 pricing models and give the key differentiator for each.
questions.answer: 1. On-Demand — pay per second/hour, no commitment, most flexible, most expensive. 2. Spot — up to 90% off, uses spare capacity, can be interrupted with 2 min notice. 3. Reserved Instances — up to 72% off, 1 or 3 year commitment, fixed instance type/region. 4. Savings Plans — up to 66% off, flexible commitment by dollar/hour, applies across instance families. 5. Dedicated Host — physical server exclusively yours, for licensing compliance or regulation.

questions.question: What state must an EC2 instance be in to change its instance type? Why?
questions.answer: The instance must be in the Stopped state. AWS needs to deallocate the current hardware and allocate new hardware matching the new instance type — this cannot happen while the server is running. Stop → change type → start.

questions.question: What is EC2 Instance Connect and how does it differ from a regular SSH connection?
questions.answer: EC2 Instance Connect is a browser-based connection method that requires no software or key file. AWS temporarily pushes a one-time public SSH key to the instance for 60 seconds, establishes the connection, then removes the key. Regular SSH uses a persistent key pair you manage yourself. Both still require port 22 open in the Security Group.

questions.question: Walk me through how you would troubleshoot an SSH connection that keeps timing out.
questions.answer: (Situation) I was trying to SSH into a new EC2 instance and the connection kept timing out rather than connecting or giving a permission error. (Task) I needed to identify and resolve the network-level block. (Action) I went to the EC2 console and checked the Security Group inbound rules — port 22 SSH was not in the list. I added an SSH rule allowing traffic from my IP on port 22. (Result) The SSH connection succeeded on the next attempt. I added this check to our EC2 launch checklist to prevent it in future.

questions.question: Describe how you would safely upgrade a production web server from t3.small to t3.large.
questions.answer: (Situation) Our web application outgrew its t3.small instance — response times degraded under load. (Task) Upgrade to t3.large with minimum service disruption. (Action) I scheduled a maintenance window. I stopped the instance during a low-traffic period, went to Actions → Instance settings → Change instance type → selected t3.large → Applied. Started the instance, waited for it to reach Running state, verified the application was responding correctly, and confirmed the instance type in the console. (Result) The upgrade completed in under 5 minutes of downtime. Load times improved significantly.

questions.question: A junior engineer accidentally terminated a production database EC2 instance. How could this have been prevented?
questions.answer: (Situation) A junior engineer accidentally clicked Terminate on the production database instance. (Task) Identify prevention measures. (Action) I implemented three layers: 1. Enabled Termination Protection on the instance. 2. Created an IAM policy restricting the ec2:TerminateInstances action to senior engineers only. 3. Set up regular AMI snapshots for recovery. (Result) Even if all other controls fail, the AMI snapshot ensures recovery within minutes.

questions.question: How would you connect to a Windows EC2 instance that you just launched?
questions.answer: (Situation) I needed to access a newly launched Windows Server EC2 instance. (Task) Establish an RDP connection. (Action) I waited 2-3 minutes for Windows to finish booting. In the EC2 console I selected the instance → Connect → RDP client tab → Get password → uploaded my .pem key file to decrypt the Administrator password → copied the password → downloaded the .rdp file. I opened the .rdp file, entered username 'Administrator' and the decrypted password, accepted the certificate warning. (Result) The Windows Server desktop appeared — I was connected.

questions.question: A customer asks why they are still being charged for their EC2 instance even though it is stopped. What do you explain?
questions.answer: (Situation) A customer believed stopping their instance stopped all charges. (Task) Clarify the billing model. (Action) I explained that stopping an EC2 instance stops compute charges (CPU/RAM) but attached EBS volumes continue to be billed at standard storage rates because the volumes persist and hold the data. The volume exists whether the instance is running or not. I showed them the EBS volumes in the console and explained they could reduce costs by creating an AMI snapshot and terminating the instance if they do not need it. (Result) The customer understood the distinction and made an informed decision about their architecture.

questions.question: Your company has a batch job that processes data every night for 4 hours. It can be safely restarted if interrupted. How do you minimise cost?
questions.answer: (Situation) A nightly 4-hour batch job was running on On-Demand EC2, costing full price. (Task) Reduce compute costs significantly. (Action) I migrated the job to Spot Instances — using a Spot request with a defined maximum price. The job was refactored to save progress checkpoints every 30 minutes so any interruption would lose at most 30 minutes of work. (Result) Compute costs reduced by approximately 85%. Over 3 months this saved thousands of dollars with no meaningful impact on job completion time.

questions.question: Explain the EC2 instance lifecycle — all states and transitions.
questions.answer: An EC2 instance follows this lifecycle: Launch → Pending (AWS provisions hardware, boots OS, no charge) → Running (instance active, compute billing starts) → from Running: Stop → Stopping → Stopped (compute charges stop, EBS charges continue; recoverable). From Running: Reboot → Running (stays on same host, same IP, brief restart). From Running: Terminate → Shutting-down → Terminated (permanent deletion, all charges stop, irreversible). From Stopped: Start → Pending → Running again. Stop/Start may assign a new public IP and potentially new physical host.

questions.question: When would you recommend Dedicated Hosts over regular EC2 instances?
questions.answer: (Situation) A financial services client ran Oracle Database workloads on EC2. (Task) Advise on hosting model for compliance and licensing. (Action) I recommended Dedicated Hosts because: 1. Oracle licenses their software per physical core — Dedicated Hosts provide visibility into exact core count for license audit compliance. 2. The client's regulatory framework required proof that no other organisation's workloads ran on the same physical hardware. (Result) The client achieved both licensing compliance and regulatory compliance, accepting the premium cost as necessary for their industry.

questions.question: What is the difference between Reserved Instances and Savings Plans?
questions.answer: (Situation) A customer needed long-term compute discounts but planned to evolve their architecture. (Task) Recommend the right commitment model. (Action) I explained: Reserved Instances lock you to a specific instance type and region (Standard RI) or instance family (Convertible RI) — up to 72% discount. Savings Plans commit to a dollar amount of usage per hour for 1-3 years but the discount applies flexibly across any instance type, OS, or size (Compute Savings Plans also cover Lambda and Fargate) — up to 66% discount. (Result) For their evolving architecture, Savings Plans gave near-equivalent savings with far greater flexibility.

questions.question: You notice an EC2 instance has 'Instance initiated shutdown behavior' set to Terminate. What risk does this create and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) During an audit, I found a production EC2 instance with shutdown behavior set to Terminate instead of Stop. (Task) Assess the risk and remediate. (Action) The risk: if anyone runs 'sudo shutdown' or 'sudo poweroff' from inside the OS — even accidentally during maintenance — the instance is permanently deleted. Fix: go to EC2 console → select instance → Actions → Instance settings → Change shutdown behavior → change to Stop → Save. Also enabled Termination Protection as a second layer. (Result) The instance is now protected from both internal and external accidental termination.

questions.question: How does the AWS Shared Responsibility Model apply to EC2 — what is AWS responsible for and what are you responsible for?
questions.answer: AWS is responsible for the physical hardware, data centre facilities, hypervisor layer, and network infrastructure — the 'security OF the cloud'. You are responsible for the OS (patching, updates), application security, Security Group configuration, IAM user permissions, key pair management, and data encryption — the 'security IN the cloud'. For EC2 specifically: you are responsible for patching your Amazon Linux or Windows OS, not AWS.

questions.question: Design a secure, highly available EC2 architecture for a web application using the concepts covered in this session.
questions.answer: Multi-AZ deployment: place EC2 instances in at least 2 Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer. Security: separate Security Groups for the load balancer (80/443 inbound from internet), web tier (80/443 from load balancer SG only), and database tier (3306/5432 from web SG only). No SSH port 22 open to 0.0.0.0/0 — use EC2 Instance Connect or AWS Systems Manager Session Manager instead. Enable Termination Protection on all instances. Use Reserved Instances for the web tier (predictable 24/7 load). Use Spot Instances for batch processing jobs. Elastic IP for any fixed-endpoint requirements.

questions.question: Compare the cost implications of keeping an EC2 instance stopped for 3 months vs terminating it, creating an AMI, and re-launching when needed.
questions.answer: Stopped for 3 months: EBS volume charges continue (typically $0.10/GB/month for gp3). A 50 GB root volume costs $5/month × 3 = $15. No compute charges. Terminate + AMI approach: EBS snapshot charges for the AMI (much cheaper than a full volume — typically $0.05/GB/month for changed blocks). Re-launch creates a fresh EBS volume from the snapshot when needed. For long periods of non-use, terminating and preserving an AMI is more cost-effective. The trade-off is launch time (2-5 minutes) vs instant availability of a stopped instance.

questions.question: A developer accidentally terminated an EC2 instance that had no termination protection. Is there any recovery path?
questions.answer: Termination is irreversible — there is no undo. Recovery options depend entirely on pre-existing backups: 1. AMI (Amazon Machine Image) — if a snapshot was taken, launch a new instance from it. Data is recovered to the point of the last snapshot. 2. EBS snapshots — if separate data volumes were snapshotted, restore them to a new instance. 3. No backup = total data loss. Prevention is the only true protection: Termination Protection + IAM restrictions + regular AMI snapshots + testing recovery procedures.

questions.question: Explain how you would architect EC2 workloads to use a combination of pricing models to minimise cost without sacrificing reliability.
questions.answer: Tiered pricing strategy: 1. Baseline capacity (always-on core load) → Reserved Instances or Savings Plans (1-3 year, 60-72% savings). 2. Variable capacity above baseline → On-Demand (flexible, no commitment needed for short spikes). 3. Batch and background processing → Spot Instances with checkpointing (up to 90% savings, acceptable interruption risk). 4. Compliance-required workloads → Dedicated Hosts (necessary premium). This combination achieves near-maximum savings on predictable load, maintains flexibility for spikes, dramatically reduces batch costs, and meets compliance requirements where needed.
